title: What we learned trying to make an LLM centered real-time game
author: Junior_Garbage4802
selftext:
Hi r/aigamedev,

We're a small indie team building **Teach My Little Sister How To Drive**, a game where you sit in the passenger seat and teach your little sister how to drive by actually talking to her. Basically, it's **rage game with AI Agent.**

Trailer: \[[LINK](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=omfip4s3mv8)\]

Steam: \[[LINK](https://store.steampowered.com/app/3948460)\]

We've spent a ridiculous amount of time testing different LLMs to make this work as an actual real-time game rather than an AI tech demo.

I thought it might be useful to share some of the things we learned.

# 0. What does the AI actually do in our game?

The basic pipeline looks like this:

**Player voice → LLM → character response + driving decision → local voice generation → gameplay**

The LLM receives the player's speech and decides both what the little sister should say and what action she should take. The game then interprets those results and makes her operate the vehicle.

Her spoken response is generated in real time using a voice generation model running locally on the player's PC.

# 1. Before using an LLM as system, your game design needs a reason for the LLM to exist

This was probably the most important design decision we made.

Why is the driver the player's **little sister**, and why is she a **beginner driver**?

Beginners sometimes do things that make absolutely no sense. They misunderstand instructions,  hesitate, and panic. Their behaviours looks remarkably similar to what happens when an LLM misunderstands your instructions.

We don't think you can just insert an LLM into an existing game and expect players to appreciate it because "AI" is technically impressive. Players are increasingly skeptical of AI features, and if the AI doesn't create something that could not reasonably exist without it, it can easily feel unnecessary.

# 2. Finding an LLM that is fast enough.

Our game is based on real-time voice conversation. Therefore, response quality and latency are most important metrics. We've tested a lot of model families and providers over the course of development: GPT models, Gemini, Mistral, Qwen, Claude, Grok, and several others including local models.

For our game, our current target response latency is **under 1.3 seconds**. The response latency means from the moment the player's utterance ends to the moment we receive enough of the LLM response to trigger the next step.

Under 1.3 secondes, players can still interpret the delay as *dumb sister*.

Once it becomes longer, that interpretation increasingly changes to a *system bug.*

So we ended up optimizing things that don't matter nearly as much in normal LLM applications. For example, geographical routing matters. For providers that offer regional routing, we route players differently depending on their country rather than sending everyone to the same endpoint.

We also found that output format matters. In our own tests, requesting structured output frequently added roughly **0.2–0.5 seconds** compared with getting a simple text response. Because of that, we currently prefer compact raw text responses for latency-sensitive actions and parse them ourselves instead of relying on structured output everywhere.

After testing a lot of options, we're currently using **Gemini 2.5 Flash** for our primary global pipeline.

# 3. We really wanted to use a local LLM. We still think it's too early for our game.

We have also tested many local models. A local LLM sounds extremely attractive for a game as it does not cost, no network connection, no network latency, solving privacy.

Unfortunately, the reality was more complicated. Our first problem is that our inputs are text and audio.

There simply haven't been that many small local multimodal models that can directly handle audio while also meeting the intelligence, latency and multilingual requirements we need.

The newer **Gemma 4 E2B / E4B** models are particularly interesting to us, and it's probably one of the closest things we've tested to what we eventually want.

But it still doesn't meet our requirements yet.

I'll probably write a separate post about our local-model experiments because there's too much to cover here.

The main issue for local models is hardware.

The bigger issue, though, is hardware.

A large percentage of gaming PCs do not have enough VRAM available. Plus, other background programs may use GPU and your game also needs it. This forces you toward smaller models.

And in our testing, models that become small enough to be comfortable for a broad gaming audience often lose too much intelligence for our gameplay. That's why we currently think fully localized LLM gameplay is still have a long way to go.

Furthermore, there are not much local small language model support more than English and Chinese. Altough these two languages are main languages used by steam users, you can't just let other language users go.

# 4. You need other AI provider for "Chinese Region"

Mainland China is second biggest market on PC game. It is enough reason why you should find Chinese AI Provider for them.

During our Steam review process, our game was restricted from mainland Chinese users. I assume it was because a core service required by the game wasn't available there.

We researched models and providers that could actually be accessed reliably from mainland China and built a separate model path for those players. We are currently using **dola seed 2.0 mini.**

# 5. Authentication

If your game directly calls an AI API from the client, you should assume that anything permanently embedded in your executable can eventually be extracted. So you need to think about authentication architecture before shipping.

If the provider doesn't support a safe client credential system for the API you're using, you may need to proxy requests through infrastructure you control instead.

In our case, we created **Firebase Functions** and **Alibaba Cloud Function Compute (for China region)** that distribute temporal api key for steam users who own the game.

# 6. So how are you guys doing so far?

Since releasing the demo, the game has gone viral in Korea and Taiwan, with videos reaching around **6 million views** so far. Plus, Japanese media also posted news for new trailer, reaching almost [3 million views in X](https://x.com/denfaminicogame/status/2085240248003690826).

We're currently aiming for a release later this year or around January, while working hard to introduce the game to more players in North America and China. The main development issue we are currently dealing with is fallback system for LLM's failure or late response.

We were also selected for **TGS 2026 Indie 80**, and next month we'll be presenting in Tokyo as one of the **Finalist 8**.

If you're coming to Tokyo Game Show, we'd love to meet and talk. Feel free to reach out on our

Discord: \[[discord](https://discord.gg/FGKPcydtty)\]

If people are interested, I can write a follow-up about another part of our pipeline like serving local voice generation model.

comments.author: Significant_Swim8994
comments.body:
Have the LLM drive longer form decisions for the sister and the allow the LLM to change the scripts driving the sisters actions. It allows the LLM to profile and anticipate the players decisions, allowing the sister to act according to quick scripted behaviours, while the LLM, which CANNOT, at least yet, act instantly.

So the LLM is slowly adapting the sisters behaviour to match/challenge the players demeanor.

comments.author: Elegant-Tangerine198
comments.body: I had an idea of LLM controlling a character years ago. The only difficulty for this genre is, whether the repeated failure of the LLM (your sister crashes the car in this game) remains interesting, rather than frustrating. If the sister never improves her skill, this game just become a series of fancy failure. I hope to see that the sister does improve when driving the same track again and solve challenges that were not able to solve.

comments.author: Evoroth
comments.body:
Point 1 is the one I wish more AI-game posts led with  - giving the model a reason to be imperfect. "She's a nervous beginner" turns the failure mode into the fantasy instead of fighting it.

On latency: we hit the same structured-output tax, and what helped most was splitting the call: a fast, constrained raw-text response for the time-critical action, and a separate slightly-slower call for the flavour/voice line that can land a beat later. Players forgive a late word far more than a late action.

And +1 on never trusting client-embedded keys - proxying through your own function with short-lived per-owner tokens is what I would do.
